6.1 Overview of Warehouse Automation Systems
In today’s fast-paced world of logistics, the demand for efficient and productive
warehouse operations has never been greater. Thankfully, the advent of
warehouse automation systems has brought about a transformative change in
the industry. By integrating cutting-edge technology and advanced robotics,
these systems have streamlined processes, minimized errors, and significantly
increased operational efficiency.
A warehouse automation system involves the implementation of different
software and technologies to automate and streamline the various processes
associated with managing and operating a warehouse. These technologies can
include AGV systems, material flow systems, WMSs, conveyor systems, robotics
systems, and automated storage and retrieval systems. Numerous businesses
across various industries are using warehouse automation to optimize their
supply chain management and improve overall productivity.
The aim of warehouse automation is to enhance the efficiency, precision, and
swiftness of warehouse tasks, while simultaneously minimizing costs and errors.
By automating inventory management, order processing, and material handling
activities, warehouse automation facilitates organizations to enhance their
supply chain management and overall productivity.
At the heart of a warehouse automation system are several key components
working in harmony to optimize every aspect of the supply chain. First and
foremost, automated storage and retrieval systems play a vital role. These
systems utilize computer-controlled mechanisms to handle the storage and
retrieval of goods, eliminating the need for manual intervention and maximizing
space utilization.
© 

363
Next, robotic picking systems have emerged as game-changers. Equipped with
sensors and advanced algorithms, these robots navigate through the
warehouse, accurately identifying and picking items for order fulfillment. By
eliminating human error and drastically reducing picking time, these systems
have revolutionized the e-commerce sector.
Conveyors and sortation systems are another integral part of warehouse
automation. These systems transport goods seamlessly throughout the
warehouse, ensuring timely and efficient movement from one area to another.
They enable continuous flow and facilitate the sorting and routing of items
based on predefined criteria, optimizing order processing.
To manage and orchestrate these complex operations, WMSs provide the
necessary intelligence. WMS software integrates with various components of the
automation system, overseeing inventory control, order processing, and real-
time tracking. This centralized control ensures smooth coordination and
enhances visibility across the supply chain.
Finally, to ensure a safe and secure working environment, AGVs have gained
prominence. These autonomous vehicles navigate through the warehouse,
transporting goods, and even interacting with other automation components.
With built-in safety measures and efficient route planning, AGVs contribute to
reducing accidents and improving operational efficiency.
Businesses can utilize various types of automation systems to streamline their
warehouse operations, which include the following:
Conveyor systems
These automated systems transport goods from one location to another
within a warehouse.
Automated storage and retrieval systems
These systems utilize computer-controlled cranes to retrieve and store
products in high-density storage systems.
Robotics systems
These systems employ robots for tasks like palletizing, depalletizing, and
order picking.
AGVs
These unmanned vehicles transport products through the picking process,
enhancing accuracy and speed.

Automated packing systems
These systems automatically package products for shipping.
Automated labeling systems
These systems label products with barcodes and other identifying
information automatically.
Sortation systems
These systems sort and distribute products according to predetermined
criteria.
Pick-to-light systems
These systems employ lights to guide workers through the picking process,
which results in higher accuracy and speed.
Pick by voice /augmented reality (AR)
This warehouse automation system uses speech recognition technology to
guide warehouse workers through the picking process.
WMSs
These systems manage and optimize warehouse operations, including
inventory management, order processing, and shipping and receiving.
In general, these automation systems can improve efficiency, increase
productivity, reduce errors, and lower labor costs for businesses.
Starting with SAP EWM 5.1, an integration option for automated warehouses has
been available. This integration allowed for the connection of programmable
logic controllers (PLCs) to various systems such as conveyor belts, rack feeders,
lifts, and more through SAP EWM.
One key aspect of integrating SAP EWM with warehouse automation systems is
the exchange of real-time data and information. Automated systems such as
conveyor belts, sorters, robots, and automated storage and retrieval systems are
equipped with sensors and other technologies that capture data on inventory
movements, order statuses, and equipment performance. This data is
seamlessly shared with SAP EWM, providing accurate and up-to-date
information for decision-making and process optimization.
By integrating with warehouse automation systems, SAP EWM can effectively
manage and orchestrate various automated processes. For example, it can
control and monitor the movement of AGVs within a warehouse, ensuring
efficient material flow and picking processes. It can also coordinate with robotic
© 

365
systems for tasks such as picking, packing, and palletizing, improving order
fulfillment speed and accuracy.
Furthermore, integration with warehouse automation systems allows SAP EWM
to optimize resource utilization and warehouse layout. The system can analyze
real-time data from automated equipment, such as storage capacity, equipment
availability, and congestion points, to make intelligent decisions on task
assignment, equipment allocation, and routing. This optimization minimizes
unnecessary movements, reduces idle time, and maximizes the use of available
resources, leading to improved throughput and operational efficiency.
Another significant benefit of integrating SAP EWM with warehouse automation
systems is enhanced traceability and visibility. Automated systems generate a
wealth of data regarding inventory movements, picking and packing processes,
and quality control. By integrating this data with SAP EWM, businesses can have
a comprehensive view of their warehouse operations in real-time. They can track
the progress of orders, identify bottlenecks, and proactively address any issues
that may arise.
Furthermore, SAP EWM can be integrated with various other warehouse
automation systems, including the following:
Material flow systems
SAP Warehouse Robotics for robotic integration
Automated storage and retrieval systems
AGVs

6.2 Material Flow Systems
A material flow system, as shown in Figure 6.1, allows for the connection of an
automatic warehouse to SAP EWM without requiring an additional warehouse
control unit. The material flow system can be configured to divide warehouse
tasks from a source location to a destination location into smaller subtasks.
These subtasks are then transmitted step-by-step to a PLC, which is a real-time
system responsible for controlling the physical transportation of handling units
(HUs) and their components on the conveyor system.
Figure 6.1 Overview of Material Flow Systems
The communication between the material flow system and PLCs is facilitated
through telegram communication. With this setup, the putaway and removal
from storage of HUs can be accomplished without the need for additional
software systems.
Business warehouses can define the capacity limits for communication points,
conveyor segments, or resources, and as a result, the SAP EWM system holds
back tasks for the PLC as soon as these limits are being approached.
A material flow system provides the following features:
Identification of HUs is automatic through scanners in the automatic storage
retrieval facility.
HUs that cannot be stored due to incorrect contours, excessive weight, or lack
of identification are automatically diverted.
© 

367
Fully automatic putaway of HUs in the storage bin is possible using any
number of interim steps.
These interim steps are represented by communication points.
Malfunctions reported by the controls are taken into account.
Capacity limits for communication points, conveyor segments, and vehicles
are taken into account.
Task interleaving is used to reduce empty traveling paths for stacker cranes.
Goods-to-person picking is available.
Stock is available for deliveries during transportation within the system.
Parallel, bidirectional communication channels ensure stable telegram
communications between SAP EWM and PLCs.
In the following sections, we’ll discuss both inbound and outbound processes of
the material flow system.
6.2.1 Inbound Process
In this section, we’ll explore inbound processes using the material flow system in
detail. The inbound process flow with a material flow system involves the
movement of materials into a warehouse. The material flow system is a module
within the SAP EWM solution for managing and optimizing material flows within
a warehouse.
Business Process
As shown in Figure 6.2, an inbound process flow with the material flow system
involves the following steps:
1. The inbound goods receipt process begins with creation of an inbound
delivery with reference to a purchase order in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA.
2. As the truck physically arrives at the warehouse, the material is physically
unloaded, and the warehouse operations team performs a goods receipt in
the SAP EWM system. The goods receipt document records the actual
receipt of the material in system and updates the inventory in SAP EWM as
well as SAP ERP system.
Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

368
3. Posting a goods receipt in SAP EWM creates a warehouse task automatically,
based on the postprocessing framework (PPF) configuration. The pallet HU
is physically loaded at the scanner area, which is mapped to
communication point. Pallet movement from the unloading area to the
scanner area or communication point will vary depending on the business
process.
4. Once the pallet HU is scanned for a weight and dimension check,
communication between the PLC/conveyor system and SAP EWM start. The
PLC communicates to SAP EWM about the current source location. SAP EWM
confirms the message is received and communicates back to the PLC
regarding the next destination location.
5. The pallet HU is moved from one communication point to another with
reference to the creation and communication of the warehouse task
between PLC and SAP EWM.
6. With the help of a crane, the pallet HU is finally putaway in an aisle bin, and
the warehouse putaway process is complete.
Throughout the inbound process flow, a material flow system provides real-time
visibility and control over material movements, ensuring efficient and accurate
handling of incoming goods within a warehouse.
Figure 6.2 Inbound Process Material Flow System

Configuration
In this section, we’ll cover the primary configuration steps needed for inbound
goods receipts using the material flow system:
1. Define the PLC interface type in SAP EWM
To accommodate various devices such as pallet conveyors, case conveyors,
single load handling devices, multiple load handling devices, shuttles,
robots, or elevators, utilizing diverse telegram types and structures may be
necessary. Thus, an interface type must be defined for each unique interface
in the warehouse. This interface type must then be assigned to each
respective PLC. Telegram structures can be established based on
warehouse, interface type, and telegram type by following the IMG menu
path SCM Extended Warehouse Management • Extended Warehouse
Management • Cross-Process Settings • Material Flow System (MFS) •
Master Data • Define PLC Interface Type. Click New Entries and maintain
the PLC interface type (Intfc.Type) or verify the existing PLC interface types
meet your business requirements, as shown in Figure 6.3.
Figure 6.3 Define PLC Interface Type
2. Define a PLC in SAP EWM
This customization activity involves defining a PLC that identifies each
communication point by its name and by its assigned PLC, which will
control these communication points. Follow the IMG menu path SCM
Extended Warehouse Management • Extended Warehouse Management •
Cross-Process Settings • Material Flow System (MFS) • Master Data •
Define Programmable Logical Control (PLC). Click New Entries and
maintain the PLC settings or verify the existing settings meet your business
requirements, as shown in Figure 6.4.

Master Data Setup

Management • Extended Warehouse Management • Master Data •
Material Flow System (MFS) • Maintain Communication Points or via
Transaction /SCWM/MFS_CP. Maintain the Storage Bin field for each
combination of PLC and communication point (Comm. Pnt.), as shown in
Figure 6.24.

Process Demo
In this section, we’ll go through an inbound goods receipt and putaway process
using a material flow system step by step:
1. Create a purchase order in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA
To create a purchase order, execute Transaction ME21N. Input the supplier,
material, purchase order quantity, plant, and receiving storage location and
other mandatory required details as required and save, as shown in
Figure 6.27. Note the purchase order number, which you’ll need for the next
step.

Figure 6.27 Create Purchase Order
2. Create an inbound delivery (with reference to purchase order)
To create an inbound delivery, execute Transaction VL31N, enter supplier
and purchase order detail and other details as needed for the business
process and click Continue and Save to generate an inbound delivery, as
shown in Figure 6.28. Note the inbound delivery number, which you’ll need
for the next step.
Figure 6.28 Create Inbound Delivery
3. Display an inbound delivery in SAP EWM
To display the details of an inbound delivery, execute Transaction
/SCWM/PRDI. In the Find field, select Inbound Delivery and enter the
inbound delivery number from earlier and click Execute. The inbound
delivery item will be displayed, as shown in Figure 6.29.

been changed to Completed, as shown in Figure 6.30.
Figure 6.30 Perform Goods Receipt

zone to the communication point CP01 and scan the HU

6.2.2 Outbound Process
In this section, we’ll go through the outbound process using the material flow
system in detail.
Business Process
The outbound process flow with a material flow system, shown in Figure 6.52,
typically involves the movement of goods from the warehouse to a production
area or a shipping area. The material flow system is a component of SAP EWM for
managing and optimizing material flows within a warehouse.
An outbound process flow with a material flow system generally involves the
following steps:
1. The outbound goods issue process begins with the creation of an outbound
delivery with reference to a sales order in SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA.
2. This outbound delivery is automatically replicated to SAP EWM, and the SAP
EWM system creates a wave with reference to the outbound delivery order.
Upon release of the wave, the pick warehouse task is getting to move the
material from the aisle bin to the outbound staging area.
3. With the SAP EWM-PLC interface, the SAP EWM system communicates to the
crane PLC to pick the pallet HU from the source aisle bin and move to the
next communication point.
4. The crane picks the pallet HU and physically moves to the next
communication point and communicates back to SAP EWM about the HU
move.

next destination location to the crane or conveyor PLC.
6. With the communication between SAP EWM and PLCs, and with reference to

moves to the outbound shipping area.
7. As the truck arrives, the loading of pallet the HU is performed, and the
warehouse operation team performs the post goods issue for the outbound
delivery order.

and enables the operation of diverse fleets using the same software stack. By
integrating the latest generation of collaborative robots with SAP EWM,

SAP Warehouse Robotics has made agile robotics more accessible by offering
the following features:
Simple setup and scalability, with the ability to quickly add additional robots
as needed to handle peak demand.
Freedom from vendor lock-in, thanks to compatibility with a wide range of
transportation robots commonly used in warehouses. This flexibility
eliminates the need for expensive integration projects.
Effortless management of diverse fleets, without the need for additional
integration efforts.
SAP Warehouse Robotics can be operated with out-of-the-box scenarios for SAP
EWM. This resource provides simplified security and IT governance, lower costs,
and easier entry into the world of warehouse robotics. Additionally, SAP
Warehouse Robotics facilitates easy robot integration and allows for the
addition of new ad-hoc robots. It also enables the management of
heterogeneous fleets in one solution, where different robots can perform
different tasks.
SAP Warehouse Robotics allows warehouses to automate operations using
robots. This approach enables HUs to be moved from source storage areas

Robotics can seamlessly integrate with warehouse robots from various vendors
with minimal variations, enabling the operation of heterogeneous fleets. This
solution provides strategic flexibility and a cost-effective entry point into the

6.4 Automated Storage and Retrieval Systems
An automated storage and retrieval system is a technology-driven solution
designed to streamline inventory management in manufacturing warehouses
and distribution centers. It integrates software technologies and hardware to
automate the process of storing and retrieving goods from storage locations.
Essentially, an automated storage and retrieval system can be thought of as a
“mini-warehouse” within a larger warehouse, with bulk storage, small racks, and
other storage areas arranged in a specific physical layout.
The automated storage and retrieval system serves several purposes, including
receiving and storing inventory from external sources, holding in-process
inventory for production lines, managing inventory levels, and facilitating the
retrieval of pallets for order picking and customer delivery.
Typically, automated storage and retrieval systems utilize various storage
technologies such as pallet racks, shelving, vertical lift modules, and carousels.
These storage units are controlled by computer software that manages
inventory and directs the movement of goods throughout the facility.
The automated storage and retrieval process begins with the arrival of goods at
the warehouse. The items are received and entered into the inventory
management system, which determines the optimal storage location based on
various factors such as size, weight, and demand. The automated storage and
retrieval system then automatically retrieves the appropriate storage unit and
transports it to a picking station where the items are removed and prepared for
shipment.
The advantages of an automated storage and retrieval system include increased
efficiency, improved accuracy, and reduced labor costs. It also helps to minimize
the amount of space required for storage, enabling companies to optimize the
use of floor space in the warehouse.
We’ll discuss the two automated storage and retrieval system integration
options in the following sections.
© 

409
6.4.1 Integration with a Material Flow System
Automated storage and retrieval systems and material flow systems are two
important systems used in the manufacturing and warehousing industry. The
automated storage and retrieval system is used for automated storage and
retrieval of goods, while the material flow system is used for managing the
material flow in a warehouse. To interface between these two systems, the
following technical details must be considered:
Communication protocol
The automated storage and retrieval system and the material flow system
communicate through a standard communication protocol. Commonly used
protocols include OPC-UA (Open Platform Communications - Unified
Architecture) and TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol).
The protocol used for communication will depend on the specific
requirements of the warehouse.
Data exchange
The automated storage and retrieval system and the material flow system
exchange data in real time. The automated storage and retrieval system
provides information on the locations and statuses of goods, while the
material flow system provides information on the demand for goods and their
destinations. The exchange of data is done through the communication
protocol, and the data is processed by the respective systems to update their
own databases.
Interface development
The interface between the automated storage and retrieval system and the
material flow system needs to be developed based on the specific
requirements of the warehouse. The interface can be developed using
middleware tools, such as production integration, or using custom-developed
software. The interface should be designed to handle the exchange of data in
real time and should be scalable to handle large volumes of data. An
automated storage and retrieval system and a material flow system can be
integrated with each other by developing an interface between them. This
interface typically involves developing custom code or middleware to
facilitate the exchange of data between the two systems. The interface may
use APIs, web services, or other integration technologies to connect the two
systems.
Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

410
System integration
Once the interface is developed, the automated storage and retrieval system
and the material flow system must be integrated. This step involves
connecting the systems to the interface, configuring the communication
protocol, and testing the interface to ensure that it is functioning correctly.
Error handling
The automated storage and retrieval system and the material flow system
must be designed to handle errors that may occur during the data exchange.
For example, if the automated storage and retrieval system fails to provide the
location of a product, the material flow system should be able to handle this
error and take appropriate action.
In summary, the interface between the automated storage and retrieval system
and the material flow system involves the development of a communication
protocol, data exchange, interface development, system integration, and error
handling. These technical details should be carefully considered to ensure that
the interface is functioning correctly and can handle the requirements of your
warehouses.
6.4.2 Integration with Automated Guided Vehicles
The integration of an automated storage and retrieval system with AGVs can
greatly enhance the efficiency and productivity of a warehouse or distribution
center. By combining the storage and retrieval capabilities of an automated
storage and retrieval system with the autonomous transportation capabilities of
AGVs, you can create a highly automated and streamlined material handling
system.
At a high level, the integration works in the following way:
Automated storage and retrieval system
An automated storage and retrieval system consists of a series of racks,
shelves, or bins that can store and retrieve items automatically. It typically
uses robotic cranes or shuttles to handle storage and retrieval tasks. The
automated storage and retrieval system is connected to a central control
system that manages inventory, tracks locations, and handles orders.
AGVs
AGVs are autonomous vehicles designed to transport goods within a
warehouse or distribution center. They can navigate throughout a facility
© 

411
using various technologies such as lasers, magnetic strips, or vision systems.
AGVs are equipped with sensors for obstacle detection and can communicate
with the central control system.
Integration
The integration between the automated storage and retrieval system and
AGVs involves coordination between the two systems. The central control
system of the automated storage and retrieval system communicates with the
AGVs to instruct them on the locations of items to be retrieved or stored.
Retrieval process
When an order is received, the central control system identifies the location of
the requested item within the automated storage and retrieval system. It then
sends instructions to the AGVs, specifying the location and item details. The
AGVs navigate to the designated rack or shelf and wait for the automated
storage and retrieval system to retrieve the item.
Item retrieval
The automated storage and retrieval system system’s robotic cranes or
shuttles retrieve the requested item from the designated storage location.
Once the item is retrieved, the automated storage and retrieval system
communicates with the AGVs to inform them that the item is ready for
transport.
Transport
The AGVs receive the signal from the automated storage and retrieval system
and navigate to the location where the item was retrieved. They load the item
onto their platforms or trailers and transport items to the desired destination,
such as a packing area or a specific workstation.
Storage process
When items need to be stored in an automated storage and retrieval system,
the central control system identifies an available storage location. It sends
instructions to the AGVs, specifying the item details and the destination rack
or shelf. The AGV transports the item to the designated location and waits for
the automated storage and retrieval system to store it.
Item storage
The automated storage and retrieval system’s robotic cranes or shuttles
receive items from AGVs and place these items in a designated storage
location within the automated storage and retrieval system. The automated
Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

412
storage and retrieval system then updates its inventory records accordingly
and communicates the completion of the storage task to the AGVs.
System optimization
The integration of automated storage and retrieval system with AGVs allows
for real-time optimization of material flows within a facility. The central
control system continuously monitors the inventory, order status, and AGV
locations to optimize the allocation of storage and retrieval tasks, minimize
travel distances, and maximize operational efficiency.
By integrating automated storage and retrieval system with AGVs, you can
achieve a seamless and efficient material handling system, reducing manual
labor, improving accuracy, and increasing overall productivity in warehousing
and distribution operations.

6.5 Automated Guided Vehicles
AGVs are autonomous vehicles used to transport materials or products within
manufacturing warehouses or distribution environments. They are equipped
with sensors, navigation systems, and control systems so they can move around
a facility without human intervention. AGVs can follow predefined paths or use
real-time mapping and localization to navigate around obstacles and other
vehicles.
The journey of AGVs has been a long one, starting from simple trucks and
culminating in modern laser-guided AGVs. An AGV is a mobile robot that follows
predefined paths or series of paths, typically along the floor of a manufacturing
or warehouse facility, to transport materials or goods. These vehicles are
designed to operate autonomously and are guided by various technologies such
as magnetic tape, lasers, or cameras.
AGVs are used in various industries such as manufacturing, automotive,
aerospace, pharmaceuticals, and logistics to move materials and products
efficiently and safely. They can be programmed to move goods between
different locations, such as between storage areas, assembly lines, or shipping
docks, without requiring human intervention.
AGVs come in different forms, including forklifts, pallet trucks, and carts, and can
be powered by batteries, electric motors, or a combination of both. Some AGVs
are equipped with sensors so they can detect obstacles in their paths and avoid
collisions, making them safe to operate around humans and other machinery.
AGVs come in many shapes and sizes, from small, simple machines to large,
complex vehicles capable of carrying heavy loads. They can be designed to
transport goods on flat surfaces, to move up and down ramps, or to enter and
exit elevators.
AGVs follow predefined paths and handle battery charging separately. On
average, in most industries, AGVs require 12 minutes of high-speed charging per
hour of usage. AGVs can adapt to options such as wireless charging, automatic
battery swaps, or solar-powered batteries to quickly get back to business.
AGVs use various forms of sensors and signals to guide them to their destination.
These sensors can range from a computer vision system that builds a real-time
Personal Copy for peerly kazes, peerlyka@cbccom.com

414
view of the plant, with obstacle detection and collision avoidance algorithms, to
a wire or coded tape on the floor defining a more static route.
While many types of AGVs and navigation methods exist on the market, they all
use some form of sensor and signal system to tell the AGV where it is located in
the space, where it needs to go, and how to get there.
Overall, AGVs are a cost-effective solution for automating material handling
tasks in various industries, improving efficiency, reducing labor costs, and
enhancing worker safety. AGVs are becoming increasingly popular in
warehouses and distribution centers due to their ability to automate material
handling tasks, increase efficiency, and reduce costs.
By integrating AGVs with SAP EWM software, material flows and warehouse
operations can be further optimized and synchronized.
To integrate AGVs with SAP EWM, follow these steps:
1. Develop a communication interface between SAP EWM and the fleet
management system (control system/guidance system) of the AGV system
manufacturer or vehicle. This step enables the distribution of warehouse
tasks to AGVs and supports the communication of warehouse task
confirmations back to SAP EWM. SAP EWM supports various communication
protocols for integrating AGVs, such as TCP/IP, XML, or APIs as well as IDoc
communication.
2. Configure the AGV as a resource in SAP EWM. AGVs are treated as resources
in SAP EWM, which can be reserved, scheduled, and tracked like any other
warehouse resource. The AGV is defined as a resource with its own set of
characteristics, such as maximum speed, capacity, and location.
3. Create and schedule AGV tasks. AGV tasks (transport requests) can be
created in SAP EWM using standard transactions or through a custom
interface. These tasks can include picking up and delivering materials,
replenishing inventory, and moving empty containers. The tasks are then
scheduled based on the availability of the AGV and the priority of the task.
AGVs physically pick up the HU from the conveyor system and deliver it to
the staging area. The SAP EWM system sends a warehouse task to the AGV,
and the AGV confirms the warehouse task back to SAP EWM as the HU
stages to the intended location specified by SAP EWM.
4. Monitor and control AGV operations. SAP EWM provides real-time visibility
into the status of AGV tasks, allowing warehouse managers to monitor and
© 

415
control AGV operations. This visibility includes tracking the AGV’s location,
speed, and battery level, as well as receiving alerts if any issues or delays
arise.
5. Integrate with other warehouse processes. AGVs can be integrated with
other warehouse processes, such as inventory management, order
management, and quality control. For example, AGVs can be used to
automatically move materials from a receiving dock to storage locations or
to transport materials from one workstation to another.
Additionally, SAP EWM can communicate with the AGV controller software using
its APIs, making it the central brain for orchestrating activity and providing a
digital command center for the entire operation, as shown in Figure 6.80.
Most companies typically initiate their integration with an AGV system by linking
it with their SAP EWM system. This connection provides insight into the
inventory available, its location within a facility, and the quantity of each item
present in a specific location.
As SAP EWM usually comes equipped with an interface, a standard operating
procedure for a minimal integration can be developed to simply record the
removal of materials from a particular location in the warehouse and its
placement onto an AGV. The AGV will then add it to the new location where it is
delivered.
Figure 6.80 AGVs
Imagine the AGV as a forklift driver given a list of items to pick. You can either
arrange the storage area such that the AGV can collect known quantities of items
on pallets, or you can have a staff member responsible for selecting and loading

If you want to integrate AGVs with your warehouse system, you must connect to

where they need to go, what they should pick up, and when they should
complete each task. Depending on the AGV supplier, you’ll either need a

with other software packages to exchange information with your AGVs.
The documentation for the AGV system will outline how this system operates.
Although the specifics may differ, the general idea is that you’ll transmit
information to the API (such as work order numbers, pick and place locations,
AGV type required for the operation, preferred routes, and schedule). The API
will then interact with the AGVs, informing them of what to do and when to do it.

7 Yard Logistics
SAP Yard Logistics, an all-encompassing software solution provided by SAP,
offers a holistic approach to optimizing and managing logistical operations
in yard or terminal settings. Its primary objective revolves around enriching
the efficiency, visibility, and coordination of inbound and outbound logistics
activities encompassing transportation, storage, and goods handling. This
chapter provides an overview of the integration between SAP Extended
Warehouse Management (SAP EWM) and SAP Yard Logistics.
Yard logistics refers to the management of operations that take place within the
confines of a shipping yard, such as a warehouse, distribution center, or freight
terminal. These operations typically involve the movement of goods, vehicles,
and personnel within the yard, as well as the storage and retrieval of items. Yard
logistics can also involve coordinating and tracking the movement of shipments,
scheduling delivery times, and managing the flow of vehicles and people in and
out of the yard. Effective yard logistics is critical for ensuring the efficient and
timely movement of goods and materials within the supply chain. Warehousing
and transportation meet at yards, which act as the connecting link.
The integration of SAP EWM and SAP Yard Logistics seamlessly facilitates the
synchronized orchestration and optimization of warehouse operations
alongside yard management. Consequently, enterprises can adeptly administer
inbound and outbound logistics processes, while adeptly handling the
movement and storage of goods within warehouse and yard premises. In
essence, the harmonious convergence of SAP EWM and SAP Yard Logistics
enables a streamlined flow of goods, engenders heightened operational
efficiency, and augments the visibility and command over warehouse and yard
undertakings. Ultimately, this amalgamation empowers organizations to attain
amplified logistics efficiency, culminating in the provision of superlative
customer service.
We’ll begin this chapter with an overview of the yard logistics process and walk
through the SAP Yard Logistics solution and its integration with SAP EWM. Then,
we’ll cover using SAP Yard Logistics in depth, detailing both inbound and
outbound processes.
